SpectralFM — label regression eval

Does the embedding beat raw input?

A frozen SSL backbone embeds each 245-point radio-telescope spectrum into a 768-dim vector. This page asks the practical question: for regressing a scalar label, does that embedding beat just using the raw 245 numbers — and specifically, does it beat raw input in the few-shot regime a foundation-model probe would actually operate in?

Overview

Label: parameter_0, the labeled_data subset (n=4,716 usable spectra, 12 unique components — 2 exact duplicates dropped). Backbone: the frozen SSL data2vec-audio checkpoint. Every number on this page passed a shuffled-label canary — refitting the identical pipeline on randomly permuted labels collapses it to ≈0, confirming nothing here is a measurement artifact.

The embedding side of this comparison was searched hard — four phases, over every block, five pooling schemes, and ten probes — specifically so a "raw input wins" verdict couldn't be blamed on an under-tuned embedding recipe.

01

The three blocks

Every result below is labeled by which block it reads from — the model's own vocabulary, not a bare tensor index:

FE
FE (pre-LN / post-LN)
5-layer conv stack. Two taps: raw output, and after feature_projection's LayerNorm.
→
Projector
Projector
Linear 512→768, plus positional conv + the encoder's pre-block LayerNorm. What Transformer layer 1 receives as input.
→
Transformer
Layer 1 – 12
12 encoder blocks. "Layer 12" is the final block's output — the conventional tap used elsewhere in this codebase.
02

Method

Raw-input baselines — three, all checked

Raw input's 245 features are highly collinear (adjacent spectral bins carry almost the same information). A standard shrinkage probe (RidgeCV) applies uniform shrinkage across all directions — which washes out signal living specifically in the thin, near-degenerate directions collinearity creates. Whitening (PCA-whitening, fit label-free on the unlabeled corpus) fixes this directly by decorrelating the feature space before the probe ever sees it.

PLS solves the same problem a different way: it looks at features and labels together and constructs a few new axes explicitly chosen to correlate with the label, no longer collinear with each other. Ordinary regression on those few axes then recovers signal RidgeCV alone never could — not because the regression got smarter, but because the hard geometric problem was already solved by the projection before regression saw the data. This is real and large at full sample size (PLS-64 and whitening land at comparable raw-input ceilings, 0.824 vs. 0.833 at 1-component). Whitening is used as the primary baseline here because it's unsupervised — free of any risk of a supervised- projection leak — and simpler to apply consistently across every sample size in the ladder below. Plain z-scoring is included too, as the "did nothing clever" floor.

Embedding recipe — searched, not assumed

Four phases, each narrowing from the last.

1

Which block

Mean-pooled, both normalizers, across all 15 blocks (FE ×2, Projector, Transformer layer 1–12). Full ranking in the scoreboard below.

2

Which pooling scheme

Tried only on the phase-1 winner: mean, mean+std, mean/max/min, four-segment (the FE's 47 output tokens split into 4 contiguous chunks, pooled separately), first+last token.

3

Concatenation

Does combining the top-2 blocks from phase 1 beat the single best block alone?

4

Which probe

Tried only on the phase 1–3 winner: RidgeCV, PLS at 4 ranks, PCA+Ridge at 3 ranks, gradient boosting, k-NN.

Protocol: RidgeCV, 5-fold CV (unless phase 4 says otherwise for the embedding). Label-efficiency ladder at n_train ∈ {10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1,000, 2,000, 4,716}, repeated random draws per rung (100 draws at n≤50, down to a single draw at the full pool), reporting the median.

scope note

The 4-phase search ran once, at 1-component, full pool. The winning recipe is reused unchanged at 2- and 3-components — it was not independently re-optimized per component count. The 2–3-component embedding numbers below are a lower bound on what a per-component search might find, not a fully independent optimum.

Signal decays steadily with Transformer depth for this task — the Projector and the first few Transformer layers are strongest; the conventional final-layer tap is the weakest Transformer-side option, beaten by every other Transformer layer and tied with the raw FE output.

Squeezing the winning block further

Pooling (phase 2, on the Projector only): four-segment pooling was clearly best — 0.918 vs. 0.858 for plain mean-pooling — splitting the sequence into four chunks before pooling captures structure a single mean discards. Concatenation (phase 3, Projector + Transformer layer 2): no improvement (0.858, identical to the Projector alone) — the two blocks carry redundant, not complementary, signal. Probe choice (phase 4, on Projector/segment4/ standardized): plain RidgeCV was the best of 10 probes tried (0.918) — PLS and PCA+Ridge at every rank tested underperformed it (0.32–0.84), likely because both discard capacity in exactly the directions where this recipe's signal concentrates, the opposite of the situation on the raw-input side.

winning embedding recipe

Projector, four-segment pooling, standardized, plain RidgeCV.

06

True vs. predicted

Full pool, axes fixed to the same range across every panel so cells are directly, visually comparable.

07

Leak check

Every configuration above was paired with a shuffled-label canary: refit the identical pipeline on randomly permuted labels. Real R² is large and positive in every case; shuffled R² is consistently ≈0 (between −0.06 and 0.00), confirming none of the reported numbers are measurement artifacts.

08

What this means

the embedding's real win

Pushed as hard as this search pushed it, the embedding's best showing is at 1-component: it overtakes raw input once there is enough labeled data (roughly n≥1,500), by a clear margin at the full pool (0.92 vs. 0.83). This is a real result, not a tie — it survived the leak canary and used a recipe found by a systematic search across 15 blocks, 5 pooling schemes, and 10 probes.

but not where it matters most

At 2- and 3-components, raw input wins at every sample size tested, including the full pool — the deeper search closed some of the gap relative to a naive mean-pooling recipe, but did not close it.

In the few-shot regime that matters most for a foundation-model probe (n≤500), raw input is ahead at every component count, including 1-component — the embedding's 1-component win only appears once labeled data is plentiful (thousands of examples), which is the opposite of "few-shot."

For the stated goal — a few-shot regressor over the embedding as a foundation-model probe — the practical conclusion is unchanged even after substantially deepening the embedding-side search: raw input remains the stronger substrate in the small-labeled-data regime, across every component count tested.

09

Recommendations

1

Use the embedding only at 1-component with ≥1,500 labels

Specifically the Projector's output, four-segment pooled, standardized, plain RidgeCV — the one regime with a genuine, leak-checked embedding advantage.

2

Use whitened raw input everywhere else

Few-shot (n≤500) at any component count, and 2–3 components at any sample size. Whitening is free (unlabeled-fit) and consistently the strongest raw-input recipe.

3

Treat the embedding's few-shot performance as still unproven

Even after this deeper search. Try stratified or active label selection (every draw here was i.i.d. random), or a per-component-count recipe search — or target a task where raw features demonstrably fail (multi-component disentangling, anomaly detection, cross-instrument transfer), since a smooth 245-point signal with a smooth scalar target is a difficult case for demonstrating an embedding's advantage.

4

Re-run this protocol on other checkpoints

In particular reconstruction-trained ones, before drawing any comparative conclusion about which checkpoint is "better" for this or a similar probing task — this study only evaluated the one SSL checkpoint above.

5

Distribution shift and calibration are untested

This study is entirely in-distribution — train and eval draws come from the same pool.

10

Reproducing this

cd code
/mnt5/noy/miniconda3/envs/spectralfm_env/bin/python3 -m eval.label_probe \
  --checkpoint /mnt5/noy/SpectralFM/checkpoints/runai/runai_long_train_2026-02-25_13-46-46.pt \
  --data /mnt5/noy/SpectralFM/fairseq/data/nova_data/labeled_data \
  --out_dir eval_outputs/label_probe/<run_name> \
  --device cuda --comps 1 2 3

The embedding-feature bank (bank.npz, several GB) is cached in out_dir and reused on a rerun with the same path — delete it to force re-extraction. Embedding extraction is a single forward pass over the full dataset (a few minutes); the 4-phase recipe search plus the label-efficiency ladders across all three component counts take several hours, dominated by repeated RidgeCV fits at the smaller sample sizes and by the phase-1 scoreboard (15 blocks × 2 normalizers, at full-pool n).
